strengths: ForeSeaQA targets a meaningful evaluation gap: surveillance question answering with reference-person images and timestamped evidence. Its six task categories, negative search examples, and potentially multiple evidence intervals offer useful coverage beyond conventional video QA.

The dataset construction pipeline is clearly motivated, attributes its UCF-Crime and UCA sources, and includes manual verification of questions, distractors, person crops, and temporal annotations. The supplementary generation prompts provide useful transparency.

ForeSea is a practical integration of existing tracking, multimodal retrieval, and video-language components. Table 1 reports improved multimodal accuracy over its VideoLLaMA3 backbone (65.4% versus 61.6%) and substantially better temporal IoU than the evaluated RAG baselines.

The ablations provide useful findings: retaining scene context helps answer accuracy, coordinate prompts can help person-focused reasoning, and global indexing improves temporal localization. The benchmark and these empirical findings have value independently of algorithmic novelty.
weaknesses: The evaluation protocol is insufficiently specified for a benchmark whose central contribution is temporal grounding. Appendix C.3 defines IoU only for single intervals, although the dataset permits multiple intervals; matching, aggregation, missing predictions, and malformed outputs are not specified. Tables 5–6 appear to macro-average task scores, whereas Section 5.1 describes averaging over questions. Furthermore, correctly predicting absence receives IoU=1, conflating rejection accuracy with localization: with balanced search positives and negatives, an always-absent predictor would obtain 50% search IoU without localizing anything. Positive-only localization and a joint answer-and-grounding metric are needed to interpret the results.

The evidence does not convincingly establish person-centric indexing as the main source of overall improvement. ForeSea-Global nearly matches multimodal accuracy (65.1% versus 65.4%), improves multimodal IoU (16.1% versus 13.8%), improves text accuracy and IoU (68.1%/18.6% versus 66.7%/13.3%), and is faster (1.4 versus 2.6 seconds). Person-centric indexing helps search, but the broader claims should reflect this narrower benefit. Against the native VideoLLaMA3 backbone, the overall gains are only 1.4 accuracy points and 0.4 IoU points, with no uncertainty estimates.

Benchmark validity and reproducibility need stronger documentation. The manuscript gives 1,041 questions but does not adequately report the number of unique source videos and identities, evaluation/development separation, annotator agreement, or annotation rejection and correction rates. Query crops are extracted from the evaluated footage, yet there is no analysis of exact-frame matching shortcuts or transfer to reference images from another time or camera. Language-only and reference-image-only controls would help establish whether the questions require the intended video reasoning.

Experimental comparisons leave important confounds unresolved. Table 3 uses different generator backbones across RAG systems, and the surveillance experiments do not sufficiently specify matched frame budgets, prompts, temporal input encoding, or baseline adaptations for image-text queries. Implementation details also omit precise detector/encoder checkpoints and tracking settings. Section 4.3 describes drawing boxes on generator inputs, whereas the selected configuration in Table 2 uses coordinates without overlays. These omissions make the reported improvements difficult to reproduce and attribute.

The generalization and scalability claims exceed the experiments. Section 5.5 replaces person-centric clips with uniformly sampled frame indexing, so its results support the broader retrieval pipeline rather than the claimed person-centric inductive bias. Comparisons use published baseline scores without a matched 90-frame uniform-sampling control. Likewise, latency measurements omit indexing cost, hardware, database scale, and variability; the evaluation does not establish performance on the hours-to-days, multi-camera search setting used to motivate the system.

The forensic deployment framing needs a substantive discussion of privacy, identity-matching errors, and unsupported accusations. Several generated questions concern roles or escalation in incidents, while temporal grounding remains weak. The absence of analysis of these failure modes limits the practical conclusions that can be drawn from multiple-choice accuracy.

strengths: ForeSeaQA targets a useful computer-vision problem: answering person-specific image-and-text queries with temporal evidence in surveillance video. The six task categories and explicit negative search examples provide a potentially valuable evaluation resource.

The pipeline is straightforward and uses appropriately cited tracking, multimodal retrieval, and video-language components. The dataset and systems contributions deserve consideration independently of whether the paper introduces a new algorithm.

The multimodal results show measurable benefits: ForeSea improves accuracy from VideoLLaMA3’s 61.6% to 65.4%, with search accuracy increasing from 49.5% to 60.5%. The supplementary retrieval comparison also supports using multimodal embeddings over CLIP for small-K retrieval.

The manuscript includes spatial-input ablations, a full-frame retrieval variant, generation prompts, and additional benchmark results. LongVideoBench performance and the reduced input-frame budget suggest that the broader retrieval framework has practical potential.
weaknesses: The evidence does not establish the central claim that person-centric indexing is the key advantage. ForeSea-Global nearly matches multimodal accuracy (65.1% versus 65.4%), improves multimodal IoU (16.1% versus 13.8%), improves both text-only metrics (68.1%/18.6% versus 66.7%/13.3%), and is faster (1.4 versus 2.6 seconds). Its average performance across query conditions also exceeds the headline system. Person-centric retrieval helps search accuracy, but the broader superiority claims need substantial qualification.

The benchmark’s aggregation protocol is inconsistent with its description. Section 5.1 describes accuracy and IoU averaged over questions, whereas Table 5’s averages match unweighted averages across task categories. Moreover, multimodal evaluation contains four categories while text-only evaluation contains six, so comparing their aggregate scores does not isolate the effect of query modality. The claimed multimodal difficulty gap requires evaluation on matched questions.

Temporal evaluation is insufficiently specified for a central benchmark contribution. Appendix C.3 defines single-interval IoU but does not explain scoring multiple predicted and ground-truth intervals, despite counting and temporal tasks requiring them. Correct negative search answers receive IoU 1, mixing absence classification with localization quality. Separate positive-event localization and negative-detection results, together with an explicit multi-interval scoring rule, are needed to interpret the reported grounding performance.

Dataset validation and reproducibility remain incomplete. Although all 1,041 questions are reportedly checked manually, the manuscript does not report the number of unique source videos or identities, annotator counts, agreement or adjudication procedures, or a human-performance estimate. Query images are cropped from the source footage, but no query-image-only or question-only controls test whether questions can be answered without examining the video. These omissions weaken confidence that the benchmark measures the intended identity and temporal reasoning.

The experimental comparisons do not cleanly isolate retrieval improvements. VideoRAG and T* use different generation backbones, and baseline frame budgets, prompting adaptations, hardware, and decoding settings are insufficiently documented. Latency excludes database construction without reporting tracking/indexing costs or storage requirements. Against the shared VideoLLaMA3 backbone, overall gains are only 1.4 accuracy points and 0.4 IoU points, with no uncertainty estimates and worse text-only performance.

Several claims exceed the demonstrated scope. Open-domain experiments replace person-centric indexing with frame retrieval plus uniform sampling, supporting the general retrieval framework rather than the proposed person-centric mechanism. The reported experiments do not establish cross-camera identity search or operation over hours-to-days archives. Implementation descriptions also conflict: Section 4.3 specifies bounding-box overlays, whereas the default ablation uses textual coordinates without overlays. These issues require clarification before the system’s contributions and reproducibility can be assessed confidently.

strengths: ForeSeaQA targets a meaningful evaluation gap: surveillance questions combining a reference image with text and requiring temporally grounded answers. The six task categories, including negative person-search queries, provide useful coverage beyond conventional video QA.

The dataset construction pipeline is clearly motivated, attributes its source videos and captions, and includes manual verification of questions, distractors, reference crops, and timestamps. The supplementary generation prompts improve transparency.

ForeSea offers a practical integration of established tracking, multimodal retrieval, and video-language models. Table 1 reports stronger multimodal accuracy than the evaluated baselines: 65.4%, versus 61.6% for its VideoLLaMA3 backbone and 61.9% for VideoRAG.

The ablations provide useful findings about preserving scene context and supplying spatial coordinates. Additional benchmarks demonstrate that the frame-retrieval variant can retain competitive video QA accuracy with a reduced input-frame budget.
weaknesses: The central evaluation protocol needs clarification. Section 5.1 describes accuracy and IoU averaged over questions, whereas the subtask tables indicate unweighted category averages. Moreover, the text-only aggregate includes Counting and Anomaly, while the multimodal aggregate does not; their difference therefore cannot directly establish the claimed difficulty of multimodal queries. Appendix C.3 assigns IoU=1 to correctly rejected negative searches, mixing absence detection with temporal localization, and does not specify how multiple predicted and reference intervals are matched. These issues affect interpretation of the benchmark's principal results.

Evidence for person-centric retrieval as the main source of improvement is mixed. ForeSea-Global achieves nearly identical multimodal accuracy (65.1% versus 65.4%), higher IoU (16.1% versus 13.8%), and lower latency (1.4 versus 2.6 seconds). It also exceeds ForeSea on both text-only metrics. The search-specific benefit is useful, but does not support broad superiority of person-centric indexing. Relative to native VideoLLaMA3, ForeSea's overall improvements are only 1.4 accuracy points and 0.4 IoU points, without uncertainty estimates.

Benchmark documentation is insufficient for assessing reliability and reproducibility: the manuscript does not clearly report the number of unique source videos and identities, development/evaluation separation, annotator counts and agreement, or the extent of manual timestamp correction. Since questions originate from captions and reference crops come from the searched footage, question-only and reference-image-only controls would help establish that performance requires the intended video reasoning.

Experimental controls and implementation details are incomplete. RAG baselines use different generation backbones, complicating attribution of gains to retrieval. Exact model checkpoints, tracking settings, surveillance frame budgets, inference prompts, timestamp mapping, and hardware are insufficiently specified. Section 4.3 describes bounding-box overlays, although the selected configuration in Table 2 uses coordinates without overlays.

The efficiency and generalization claims need narrower scope. Reported latency excludes database construction and provides no indexing-cost or database-scale analysis. Open-domain experiments replace person-centric tracking with frame-level retrieval, so they support the broader retrieval framework rather than transfer of the central person-centric design. Comparisons against published results also lack a controlled 90-frame uniform-sampling baseline.

The benchmark and system are promising, and using off-the-shelf components is not itself a weakness. However, the manuscript's multi-camera forensic-search framing exceeds its demonstrated single-video evaluation, and practical claims need discussion of identification errors, privacy, and human verification. Together with the unresolved evaluation and reproducibility issues, the current evidence supports a slight preference for rejection.

strengths: The strongest contribution is ForeSeaQA: combining reference-person images, surveillance questions, and temporal evidence addresses a useful evaluation gap. Although no contribution type is explicitly declared, the work is best assessed primarily as Datasets/Benchmarks with an Applied/Systems baseline; the use of existing components is therefore not itself a weakness.

The dataset construction includes meaningful quality control: human reviewers check all generated questions, discard approximately half the initial candidates, and correct flagged images and timestamps. Source datasets and component methods are attributed, and generation prompts are supplied.

The experimental coverage is substantial, including multiple model families, retrieval encoders, spatial-prompt configurations, global/person/hybrid retrieval, and matched-backbone comparisons. Table 3 supports a real temporal-grounding benefit: with VideoLLaMA3, ForeSea-Hybrid obtains 18.4% IoU versus VideoRAG's 9.9%.

The ablations provide useful practical observations, particularly that cropping can remove necessary context and that global evidence complements person-centric retrieval. Open-domain results also suggest that retrieval can preserve much of the backbone's accuracy with fewer input frames.
weaknesses: The benchmark's central temporal metric is insufficiently specified and potentially misleading. Appendix C.4 assigns IoU=1 to correctly rejected negative search queries; because search is balanced, always predicting absence earns 50% search IoU without localizing anything. Positive-only localization and negative rejection should be reported separately. Furthermore, the benchmark permits multiple evidence intervals, but the metric defines only single-interval IoU, without explaining interval matching, aggregation, or malformed-output handling. Separate accuracy and IoU also do not establish that correct answers have correct supporting evidence.

The reported aggregation conflicts with the evaluation description. Section 5.1 describes averaging over questions, whereas the subtask tables reproduce equal-weight task averages: ForeSea's multimodal accuracy is (60.5+60+85+56)/4=65.4%. Text evaluation additionally includes counting and anomaly, while multimodal evaluation does not. Consequently, comparing their aggregate scores does not isolate the effect of adding an image, as claimed in Section 5.2. A paired comparison over the same questions and an explicit aggregation rule are needed.

Important benchmark validation details are missing: the number of unique source videos and identities, source-video selection and splits, separation of configuration tuning from evaluation, annotator counts and agreement, and a clear dataset/evaluation-code release plan. With only 1,041 questions, potentially including paired modality versions, uncertainty estimates accounting for shared videos are particularly relevant to the small accuracy differences. Caption-only baselines do not replace question-only or reference-image-only controls for shortcut detection.

The headline accuracy advantage is not sustained under the matched-backbone comparison already provided. Table 3 shows VideoRAG with VideoLLaMA3 achieving 68.1% overall accuracy and 67.9% multimodal accuracy, exceeding default ForeSea's 66.0% and 65.4%. Thus, the repeated best-accuracy claims and the abstract's comparison against the weaker VideoRAG configuration overstate the evidence. The supported benefit is primarily a grounding–accuracy tradeoff.

Evidence for person-centric retrieval as the principal advantage is mixed. ForeSea-Global improves overall accuracy and IoU over default ForeSea (66.6%/17.4% versus 66.0%/13.6%) and is faster (1.4 versus 2.6 seconds). Open-domain experiments remove person-centric indexing entirely, so they validate generic frame retrieval rather than the distinctive surveillance design. Multi-camera identity continuity and hours-to-days retrieval are also not evaluated; benchmark videos average approximately six minutes.

Reproducibility and efficiency reporting remain incomplete. The manuscript does not adequately specify surveillance frame budgets, tracking and segmentation settings, inference prompts, timestamp mapping, hardware, or timing variability. Section 4.3 describes drawing boxes, although the default ablation uses textual coordinates without overlays. Reported latency excludes database construction, and the half-frame generalization claim lacks a matched 90-frame uniform-sampling baseline. These gaps limit confidence in the practical efficiency claims.

strengths: ForeSeaQA targets a useful combination of reference-image queries, surveillance video QA, and temporal evidence across six tasks. The benchmark and practical system integration have value independently of introducing a new algorithm.

The data pipeline includes human verification of all generated QA pairs, rejection of approximately half the initial generations, and manual correction. The supplementary generation prompts and attribution of source datasets and components support transparency.
The experimental coverage is substantial: multiple video LMMs, retrieval baselines, spatial-conditioning ablations, alternative encoders, global/hybrid retrieval, and backbone-controlled comparisons.

The controlled comparisons support a temporal-grounding benefit. In Table 3, ForeSea-Hybrid improves overall IoU over VideoRAG from 9.9% to 18.4% with VideoLLaMA3, and from 3.5% to 11.4% with LLaVA-Video.
weaknesses: The benchmark's central grounding evaluation needs stronger specification and validation. Appendix C.4 assigns IoU=1 to correctly rejected negative search queries; with balanced positives and negatives, always predicting absence would obtain 50% search IoU without localizing anything. Positive-only localization and negative rejection should therefore be reported separately. The metric description also does not specify how multiple predicted and ground-truth intervals are matched or aggregated, despite multi-interval evidence being a stated contribution. Separate answer accuracy and IoU do not establish that correct answers have correct supporting evidence.

The headline accuracy superiority is contradicted by the stronger controlled baseline already included in Table 3. VideoRAG with the same VideoLLaMA3 backbone achieves 68.1% overall accuracy and 67.9% multimodal accuracy, exceeding ForeSea's 66.0% and 65.4%, respectively, and ForeSea-Hybrid's overall 66.9%. The abstract's 3.1-point accuracy improvement depends on comparison against a different generator. The grounding improvement remains meaningful, but the main conclusions should distinguish it from accuracy superiority.

Evidence that person-centric indexing is the principal contribution is mixed. Global retrieval achieves higher overall accuracy and IoU than default ForeSea (66.6%/17.4% versus 66.0%/13.6%), and lower online latency (1.4 versus 2.6 seconds). Person-centric retrieval helps selected search results, but its general advantage is not established. The external benchmark experiments replace person-centric clips with frame indexing, so they support the broader retrieval pipeline rather than transfer of the person-centric design.

The benchmark is insufficiently characterized for assessing its reliability. The manuscript reports 1,041 questions but does not clearly document the number of distinct source videos and people, development/evaluation separation, annotator counts, agreement, or an independent annotation-quality audit. Query crops come from the source video, but no query-image-only, question-only, or mismatched-image controls establish how much performance requires identifying the referenced person across time. Caption-only experiments do not resolve these possible shortcuts.

The modality comparison is confounded by task composition. Multimodal results cover four person-specific tasks, whereas text-only results also include counting and anomaly. Consequently, their aggregate difference cannot directly establish that multimodal input is harder. Moreover, the reported averages in Tables 6–7 match unweighted task averages, while Section 5.1 describes accuracy and IoU over questions. The aggregation protocol and question counts need explicit reconciliation; uncertainty estimates are also important for the small reported gains.

Reproducibility and efficiency evidence remain incomplete. Exact detector/checkpoint settings, tracking and clip segmentation rules, surveillance frame budgets, timestamp mapping after clip concatenation, inference prompts, and latency hardware are insufficiently documented. Section 4.3 describes drawing boxes, whereas the default ablation configuration uses textual coordinates without overlays. The latency table measures retrieval and generation but omits tracking/index construction, limiting claims of end-to-end efficiency.

The practical forensic-search framing exceeds the demonstrated setting. Videos average about six minutes and reach approximately 35 minutes; no cross-camera identity-association or hours-to-days corpus-search evaluation is reported. These limitations do not invalidate the benchmark, but they leave the broader deployment and scalability claims unsupported.

strengths: ForeSeaQA targets a useful computer-vision problem: answering person-specific image-and-text queries with temporal evidence in surveillance video. Combining six task categories, reference images, and potentially multiple evidence intervals offers value beyond ordinary video QA.

The contribution is best assessed primarily as Datasets/Benchmarks with an Applied/Systems component, rather than Algorithms/General. Its value lies in the evaluation setting and integrated baseline; using existing tracking, embedding, and generation models is appropriate.

The data construction process includes meaningful quality control: manual verification, removal of approximately half the initial generations, and correction of query images and timestamps. The supplement provides generation prompts, and the source datasets and component methods are attributed.

Matched-backbone experiments support improved temporal grounding. In Table 3, ForeSea-Hybrid reaches 18.4% IoU versus VideoRAG's 9.9% with VideoLLaMA3, and improves both accuracy and IoU with LLaVA-Video. Ablations covering spatial cues, retrieval scope, encoders, and generators help substantiate the system contribution.
The global retrieval variant provides a promising efficiency result, and the external benchmark experiments suggest that selecting a compact set of frames can preserve long-video QA performance.
weaknesses: The central temporal-grounding evaluation needs stronger validation. Appendix C.4 assigns IoU=1 to correctly rejected negative search queries. Because search is balanced, always predicting absence achieves 50% search IoU without localizing anything. Consequently, aggregate IoU mixes rejection and localization ability. Positive-only localization and separate rejection metrics are needed. The scoring rule for multiple predicted and ground-truth intervals is also unspecified despite multi-interval evidence being a key benchmark feature.

Benchmark documentation is insufficient for assessing reliability and reuse. The manuscript reports 1,041 questions but does not clearly specify the number of unique videos and identities, video selection and evaluation splits, annotator counts or agreement, or independent temporal-annotation quality. It also lacks a clear dataset/code availability and release-license statement. These omissions matter particularly when the benchmark is the principal contribution.

Several headline claims exceed the controlled evidence. With the same VideoLLaMA3 backbone, VideoRAG achieves higher overall accuracy than ForeSea-Hybrid, 68.1% versus 66.9% (Table 3), so the headline accuracy advantage depends on baseline configuration. Moreover, ForeSea-Global exceeds person-centric ForeSea in overall accuracy and IoU, weakening the claim that person-centric retrieval drives the overall grounding improvement. The evidence supports a grounding–accuracy tradeoff more clearly than general superiority.

The text-versus-multimodal comparison is confounded by task composition: the multimodal average covers four person-specific tasks, whereas the text average also includes counting and anomaly. Thus, the aggregate accuracy drop cannot directly establish difficulty caused by adding a reference image. Matched-question comparisons, image-removal or image-shuffling controls, and question-only baselines would better establish whether the benchmark requires identity-grounded visual reasoning.

The practical scope and efficiency claims require qualification. Videos average about six minutes and reach roughly 35 minutes; there is no demonstrated multi-camera identity search across hours or days. External benchmark experiments replace person-centric indexing with global frame retrieval, so they validate the broader retrieval strategy rather than transfer of the central surveillance mechanism. Latency reporting omits hardware and offline tracking/index-construction costs, and the description of bounding-box overlays conflicts with the default coordinates-only configuration in Table 2.
